newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss government ready to act on Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: Swiss government ready to act on Holocaust fund.

text.p: Interior minister Ruth Dreifuss said on Sunday the Swiss government would waste no time in deciding on a memorial fund for victims of the Holocaust.
In an interview in the Swiss Sunday paper SonntagsZeitung, Dreifuss said the Federal Council (cabinet), was aware of the need to move swiftly and it was ready to take action.
"It is quite clear to the council that something has to be done fast," Dreifuss told the SonntagsZeitung.

Dreifuss also repeated that the council was not planning to denounce recent remarks by economics minister Jean-Pascal Delamuraz, who had described calls for a quick Swiss restitution to Holocaust victims as blackmail.
"Normally the council as a collective group does not correct statements made by individual members," Dreifuss said, noting such a move was not part of the country's political custom.
Most Swiss seem to agree the government should not denounce Delamuraz, nor should he resign, according to recent polls.

A survey by the Lucerne-based LINK institute, published by the Blick tabloid on Saturday, showed that less than one-third of the Swiss surveyed thought the government should distance itself from Delamuraz.
Another survey, by Sunday paper SonntagsBlick, showed that 80 percent of respondents did not think Delamuraz should resign, while 10 percent called for his resignation.
Dreifuss said she regretted that Delamuraz' remarks had led to a deterioration in the confidence and trust that had been built up between Switzerland and groups abroad.

Delamuraz's remarks, made as he was completing his one-year term in the rotating Swiss presidency, outraged Israeli politicians and world Jewish groups, who threatened to call a boycott against Swiss banks.
Two days after his remarks, Delamuraz said he was sorry if his remarks had offended any survivors of the Holocaust and he regretted if they had lead to any misunderstandings.
On Friday Swiss President Arnold Koller also made clear the government did not plan to apologise for Delamuraz' remarks.

Dreifuss noted that Switzerland was not only the country having to face its actions towards Jews during and before World War Two. Sweden, Norway, Hungary and also France faced similar problems, but some of these countries had already set up funds.
"We are also ready to take action," Dreifuss said.
The government has already acknowledged that it might compensate Jewish victims of the Nazis before the final results of a full inquiry -- which could take years -- was completed.
The Swiss people also agree a Holocaust fund should be set up, but most think it should first be done after the inquiry.
Sixty percent of the respondents in SonntagsBlick's poll agreed a fund should be created, but only after the inquiry has been completed. Fifteen percent said a fund should be set up immediately.

Groups led by the World Jewish Congress (WJC) say Swiss banks and government profited cynically from the Holocaust by sitting on accounts left ownerless by Jewish victims and by buying stolen gold from Nazi Germany during World War Two.
